paper.central_claim: ARIA: an LLM agent that learns at test time by (i) assessing its own uncertainty through structured self-dialogue to decide when to ask a human expert, and (ii) integrating the expert guidance into a timestamped, status-flagged knowledge repository with conflict/outdated detection and clarification queries, giving significant accuracy/adaptability gains over offline fine-tuning, RAG, self-improving agents and active-learning baselines on TikTok Pay CDD name screening and CUAD, and is deployed in production.
paper.title: Enabling Self-Improving Agents to Learn at Test Time With Human-In-The-Loop Guidance

evidence.quote:
First, the effectiveness of ARIA is intrinsically linked to the
availability, quality, and scalability of human expertise
. The framework assumes access to responsive and accurate human experts. In scenarios with very high query volumes, or where expert feedback is delayed, inconsistent, or erroneous, ARIA’s learning capability and overall performance could be significantly impacted. The practical cost and logistical challenges of maintaining a pool of readily available experts for diverse and evolving tasks are also important considerations not fully explored
Sui et al. (2024a)
.

Second, the
complexity of knowledge representation and conflict resolution
could pose challenges as the knowledge repository (KR) grows in size and intricacy. While ARIA incorporates mechanisms for timestamping and managing conflicting information, highly nuanced, subtly contradictory, or deeply contextual expert guidance might be difficult to integrate perfectly. Ensuring the long-term coherence and accuracy of a large, evolving KR, and preventing the accumulation of outdated or overly specific knowledge, remains an ongoing research area.
evidence.support_explanation: 专家可靠性、规模及大 KR 冲突均为作者承认边界。

evidence.quote:
Fourth, the evaluation on the public CUAD dataset relied on an
LLM-simulated human expert oracle
. Although this approach facilitates scalable experimentation, it may not fully replicate the nuances, potential biases, occasional errors, or the depth of insight that a genuine human domain expert would provide. The dynamics of interaction and the nature of guidance from a simulated oracle might differ from real-world human-agent collaboration, potentially affecting the observed learning patterns.

Finally, the
efficiency of the self-dialogue and knowledge management processes
could become a concern in applications with extremely high throughput or stringent real-time constraints. While crucial for ARIA’s adaptability, the computational overhead associated with structured self-reflection, semantic retrieval from the KR, and conflict resolution mechanisms might need further optimization for certain deployment scenarios. The current study focuses more on the effectiveness of learning rather than a detailed analysis of computational performance under heavy load.
evidence.support_explanation: 模拟 oracle 与未详细分析计算开销限制外推。

evidence.quote:
Efficiency Analysis.

As shown in Table
3
, the ARIA demonstrates significant efficiency gains compared to conventional human expert evaluation in CDD name screening tasks. The previous online method for this business was solely human evaluation. In real business, human experts typically take around 12 minutes for Average Handling Time (AHT) per case.
In contrast, ARIA’s AHT is substantially lower, even as the query budget (B) increases.
Even when ARIA is allowed to query as many questions as possible (B=3121, referred to as Full Oracle Access), its AHT is only 0.41 minutes.
This indicates a considerable time saving.
It’s also noted that for human experts, reviewing a case from scratch is time-consuming, whereas answering a query from an agent is much faster.
evidence.support_explanation: 报告平均处理时间，但问答与全量人工复核职责不同，未完整计模型维护和人工成本。

gap.author_gap: LLM agents struggle where rules and domain knowledge change frequently (regulatory compliance, risk screening); offline fine-tuning and standard prompting cannot adapt during operation.
gap.checked_gap: Real operational problem with a concrete instance (CDD name screening, watchlist/regulation updates). The static pieces are the knowledge store and when to ask for help. Drift itself is not measured in the TikTok stream (no rule-change annotation, no per-phase curves).
gap.lineage/closest_adjacent: Baselines named in paper: Reflexion (verbal reflection into episodic memory), static RAG with pre-populated KB, uncertainty-sampling active learning, Self-Refine, Multi-Agent Debate. Related Work (2.1) groups ICL/RAG/test-time fine-tuning/self-learning agents without engaging editable-memory agents with add/update/delete operations.
gap.residue: Stale and contradictory human-supplied rules accumulating in a store that is retrieved by similarity; budgeted human attention.
gap.stakes: Compliance errors (missed matches) and high manual handling time (12 min per case).
gap.method_response: Timestamps + status flags + LLM conflict comparison + clarification queries + recency-weighted retrieval; self-dialogue-triggered escalation.
gap.remaining_gap: No test that conflict handling beats simply retrieving recent entries; no evidence under real rule changes; human-expert dependency.
unresolved: Editable-memory agent neighbors not in pinned materials; novelty of status-flag conflict handling vs those not verifiable here
Whether TikTok stream contains actual rule drift

M.reason: Both seats 3; re-checked. Self-dialogue escalation, timestamped status transitions and the multiplicative validity×recency×relevance read (Eq. 3) are reconstructable and give distinguishable predictions against simple uncertainty and static RAG; verbal-confidence informativeness and LLM comparator accuracy remain assumptions.

X.reason: Opus sides with son55. The retention chain the rubric names for X is explicit: admission (expert-asserted items, §4.3 step 1–2), versioning (timestamps, Valid/PotentiallyOutdated/Superseded, superseded_by links), conflict/expiry handling with clarification queries, and the next-step read path (Eq. 3), illustrated end-to-end in App. B–C. What is missing — τ_sim, w_po, λ, N_top values, a non-human admission gate, and the future-tense CUAD instantiation (opus:O05) — limits exact reconstruction, but the CUAD protocol defects are scored once in E.measurement (A2), not again here.

E.measurement.reason: Opus sides with son55, adding defects neither seat recorded. Sensitivity/specificity suit the 156/11,690 imbalance, but TikTok label provenance is undocumented, the CUAD oracle model is unnamed (opus:O04), the CUAD protocol is a future-tense plan with optional drift steps (opus:O05), and its fine-tuned baseline (App. D.6, BERT-variant on the first stream portion) is not the Qwen2.5-7B budget-swept row reported in Table 4 (opus:O02, opus:O03). What was measured on CUAD is therefore not pinned; queried-case scoring is charged to E.holdout (A2).

E.causality.reason: Both seats 2; re-checked. Equal-budget random/uncertainty querying, an information-matched static RAG KB and four component removals give partial attribution, but there is no KR-off ARIA, Labels-Only ARIA ≈ Simple Uncertainty (feedback richness per query is a live alternative, opus:O08), temporal weighting has a null sensitivity effect (opus:O09), and autonomous self-improving baselines receive no human feedback.

E.holdout.reason: Both seats 1; re-checked. Learning stream = evaluation stream, no frozen-KR later period, the CUAD oracle is simulated and its drift synthetic, and whether expert-answered cases count toward the score is unstated while App. C shows post-guidance final outputs (opus:O01); full-oracle access reaching only 0.9428 sensitivity suggests pre-guidance scoring but the paper does not say so.

E.statistics.reason: Both seats 1; re-checked (A2 rung 1). Denominators and imbalance are given and weaker variants reported, but every cell is a single run of one stream order; one TikTok positive is 0.64 sensitivity points, so several ablation margins are 1–5 cases.

E.cost.reason: Opus sides with sol. The paper's own budget axis — expert queries — is matched across interactive baselines and swept over four levels, CUAD charges richer queries 2–3 label units (opus:O06), and handling time vs human review is reported. Not higher: LLM calls/tokens for self-dialogue, comparison and retrieval are unreported and the authors disclaim compute analysis, and TikTok charges every query type 1 (opus:O07). son55's uniform-cost point is answered on CUAD only, so 2 rather than 3.
